reminder: A holomorphic extension of $f$ is a holomorphic function on a larger domain that agrees with $f$ on the smaller domain.
definition: Let $f$ be a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on an [open set](c:open-set) $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}^n$. A holomorphic extension of $f$ to an open set $V\supsetneq U$ is a holomorphic function $F$ on $V$ with $F|_U=f$. If $V$ is [connected](c:connected-space), the identity theorem makes $F$ the only such extension.
examples: The series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n$ is holomorphic on $|z|<1$, and $1/(1-z)$ is its holomorphic extension to $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{1\}$.

Bochner's tube theorem: a holomorphic function on the [tube domain](c:tube-domain) over a connected open set $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ has a holomorphic extension to the tube over the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of $B$.
Non-example: $f(z)=1/z$ on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ has no holomorphic extension to $\mathbb{C}$, because $|f(z)|\to\infty$ as $z\to0$.

steps: Let $U\subseteq V$ be connected open sets in $\mathbb{C}$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on $U$.
An [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) of $f$ to $V$ is a holomorphic function on $V$ that equals $f$ on $U$.
That function is a holomorphic extension of $f$ to $V$.
The general notion also allows several complex variables.
links.why: It shows that an analytic continuation is the one-variable case of a holomorphic extension.

reminder: The hom-set of two objects is the set of all morphisms from the first object to the second.
definition: In a [locally small](c:locally-small) [category](c:category) $C$, the hom-set $\mathrm{hom}(x,y)$ of two [objects](c:object) $x$ and $y$ is the set of all morphisms $f:x\to y$. Composition gives maps $\mathrm{hom}(y,z)\times\mathrm{hom}(x,y)\to\mathrm{hom}(x,z)$.
examples: In the category of sets, $\mathrm{hom}(X,Y)$ is the set $Y^X$ of all functions from $X$ to $Y$.
In a poset seen as a category, $\mathrm{hom}(x,y)$ has one element if $x\le y$ and no element otherwise.
In a group seen as a category with one object, the hom-set is the underlying set of the group.
Non-example: if a category has a proper class of morphisms from $x$ to $y$, this collection is a hom-class and not a set, so the category is not locally small.

steps: In an [enriched category](c:enriched-category) over a monoidal category $V$, each pair of objects has a hom-object in $V$.
Take $V$ to be the category of sets with the cartesian product.
A hom-object in $V$ is then a set of morphisms, which is a hom-set.
links.why: It shows that hom-sets are the hom-objects of ordinary categories, which are enriched in sets.

steps: Take the category of sets, whose morphisms are functions.
The morphisms from $X$ to $Y$ are the functions $X\to Y$.
So $\mathrm{hom}(X,Y)$ is the [function set](c:function-set) $Y^X$.
links.why: It shows that a function set is the hom-set of the category of sets.

reminder: A homology $n$-sphere has the same ordinary homology groups as the $n$-sphere.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a homology $n$-sphere when $H_k(X;\mathbb{Z})\cong H_k(S^n;\mathbb{Z})$ for every $k$, where $S^n$ is the [sphere](c:sphere) and $H_k$ is [ordinary homology](c:ordinary-homology). The space $X$ need not be [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to $S^n$. Often one also asks that $X$ be a closed manifold.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ is a homology $n$-sphere.
The [Poincaré homology sphere](c:poincare-homology-sphere), the quotient of $SU(2)$ by the binary icosahedral group, is a $3$-manifold with the homology of $S^3$ and a non-trivial fundamental group.
Non-example: the real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^3$ has $H_1=\mathbb{Z}/2$, so it does not have the homology of $S^3$.

steps: Take the sphere $S^n$ itself.
Its homology groups equal those of $S^n$, so $S^n$ is a homology sphere.
A homology sphere keeps only this homology condition and drops the homeomorphism to $S^n$.
links.why: It shows that a homology sphere is a space that looks like a sphere to homology, and no more.

steps: Let $X$ be a [homotopy sphere](c:homotopy-sphere), a space with a homotopy equivalence $X\to S^n$.
A homotopy equivalence induces an isomorphism on every homology group.
So $X$ has the homology groups of $S^n$ and is a homology sphere.
The converse fails, because the Poincaré homology sphere has a non-trivial fundamental group.
links.why: It shows that homology spheres are a larger class than homotopy spheres.

reminder: A homomorphism is a map between two algebraic structures of the same type that preserves their operations.
definition: Let $A$ and $B$ be [algebraic structures](c:algebraic-structure) of the same type, for example two groups or two rings. A homomorphism is a [function](c:function) $f:A\to B$ with $f(a\ast a')=f(a)\ast f(a')$ for every [binary operation](c:binary-operation) $\ast$ of the structure. It also sends each constant of the structure, such as the unit, to the matching constant of $B$.
examples: The map $\exp:(\mathbb{R},+)\to(\mathbb{R}_{>0},\cdot)$ is a group homomorphism, because $e^{a+b}=e^ae^b$.
The determinant $\det:GL_n(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}^\times$ is a homomorphism of groups, and the reduction $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n$ is a homomorphism of rings.
Non-example: the map $f(x)=x+1$ on $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ is not a homomorphism, because $f(a+b)=a+b+1$ but $f(a)+f(b)=a+b+2$.

steps: Take a homomorphism $f:A\to B$.
Add the condition that $f$ is a bijection.
Then the inverse map $f^{-1}$ is also a homomorphism, so $f$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism).
links.why: It shows that an isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism, with no extra check on the inverse.

steps: Let $f$ be a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism), so $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$.
A group is an algebraic structure with one binary operation, and $f$ preserves it.
So $f$ is a homomorphism of algebraic structures.
The general notion also covers rings, modules and algebras.
links.why: It shows that a group homomorphism is a homomorphism for the structure of a group.

reminder: The homotopy category of a category with weak equivalences is the universal category in which every weak equivalence becomes an isomorphism.
definition: Let $C$ be a [category with weak equivalences](c:category-with-weak-equivalences), for example spaces with the [weak homotopy equivalences](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence). The homotopy category $\mathrm{Ho}(C)$ is the [localization](c:localization-of-a-category) of $C$ at the weak equivalences: a category with a functor $C\to\mathrm{Ho}(C)$ that makes every weak equivalence invertible, universally. For spaces, a morphism from a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) $X$ to a space $Y$ is a [homotopy](c:homotopy) class of continuous maps $X\to Y$.
examples: In the homotopy category of spaces, the inclusion $\{0\}\to[0,1]$ is an isomorphism, because it is a homotopy equivalence.
The [derived category](c:derived-category) $D(A)$ of an abelian category is the homotopy category of chain complexes, with the quasi-isomorphisms as weak equivalences.
If the only weak equivalences are the isomorphisms, the homotopy category is the category $C$ itself.
Non-example: the category of spaces and continuous maps is not its own homotopy category, because two homotopic maps stay different morphisms there.

steps: Start with the homotopy category $\mathrm{Ho}(C)$ of a category $C$ with weak equivalences $W$.
By definition, it comes with a functor $C\to\mathrm{Ho}(C)$ that inverts $W$ in the universal way.
So $\mathrm{Ho}(C)$ is the [localization](c:localization-of-a-category) of $C$ at $W$.
The homotopy case adds that $W$ is a class of weak equivalences, often from a model structure.
links.why: It shows that the homotopy category is a localization, so its maps are zigzags or homotopy classes.

steps: Let $A$ be an abelian category, and let $C$ be the category of chain complexes over $A$.
Call a chain map a weak equivalence when it is a quasi-isomorphism.
The homotopy category of this category with weak equivalences is the [derived category](c:derived-category) $D(A)$.
links.why: It shows that the derived category is one case of a homotopy category.

reminder: A map has the homotopy extension property when every homotopy out of its domain extends to a homotopy out of its codomain.
definition: A [continuous](c:continuous-function) map $i:A\to X$ has the homotopy extension property with respect to a [topological space](c:topological-space) $Y$ when the following holds. For every map $f:X\to Y$ and every [homotopy](c:homotopy) $h:A\times[0,1]\to Y$ with $h(a,0)=f(i(a))$, there is a homotopy $H:X\times[0,1]\to Y$ with $H(x,0)=f(x)$ and $H(i(a),t)=h(a,t)$. A map with this property for every space $Y$ is a [Hurewicz cofibration](c:hurewicz-cofibration).
examples: The inclusion of a subcomplex into a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) has the property for every space $Y$, for example $S^{n-1}\to D^n$.
The inclusion $\{0,1\}\to[0,1]$ has it: a map on $[0,1]$ and a homotopy of its two end points extend to a homotopy of the whole interval.

Non-example: the inclusion of $A=\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\}$ into $[0,1]$ fails for $Y=[0,1]\times\{0\}\cup A\times[0,1]$, because a solution would be a retraction of the square onto $Y$, and none exists.

steps: Let $i:A\to X$ have the homotopy extension property with respect to one space $Y$.
Ask for the same extensions for every space $Y$.
A map with this stronger property is a [Hurewicz cofibration](c:hurewicz-cofibration).
links.why: It shows that a Hurewicz cofibration is a map with the extension property for all test spaces at once.

reminder: A homotopy fixed point is a point that the group action fixes only up to coherently chosen homotopies.
definition: Let a topological group $G$ act on a space $X$ by a [group action](c:group-action), and let $EG$ be a [contractible space](c:contractible-space) with a free $G$-action. The space of homotopy fixed points is $X^{hG}=\mathrm{Map}_G(EG,X)$, the space of [equivariant](c:equivariant) maps $EG\to X$, and a homotopy fixed point is a point of this space, a refinement of a [fixed point](c:fixed-point). Equivalently, $X^{hG}$ is the [homotopy limit](c:homotopy-limit) of the diagram over $BG$ that the action defines.
examples: For the trivial action of $G$ on $X$, we have $X^{hG}=\mathrm{Map}(BG,X)$, so $X^{h\mathbb{Z}}$ is the free loop space of $X$.
If $G$ acts on a discrete set $X$, then $X^{hG}$ is the ordinary set $X^G$ of [fixed points](c:fixed-point), because $EG$ is connected.

Non-example: the ordinary fixed points are not the homotopy fixed points in general; for the antipodal action of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ on the contractible space $S^\infty$, the first set is empty and the second is contractible.

steps: Let $G$ be a discrete group acting on a discrete set $X$.
The space $EG$ is connected, so every $G$-equivariant map $EG\to X$ is constant.
Its value is a point of $X$ fixed by every element of $G$.
So $X^{hG}$ is the set of fixed points, and the homotopy version also works for spaces that are not discrete.
links.why: It shows that homotopy fixed points refine ordinary fixed points and agree with them for discrete sets.

steps: A $G$-action on $X$ is a diagram of shape $BG$ in spaces.
The [homotopy limit](c:homotopy-limit) of this diagram is the space of $G$-equivariant maps from $EG$ to $X$.
That space is $X^{hG}$, so homotopy fixed points form one kind of homotopy limit.
links.why: It shows that every fact about homotopy limits applies to homotopy fixed points.

reminder: The homotopy group $\pi_k(S^n)$ is the group of homotopy classes of base-point preserving maps from $S^k$ to $S^n$.
definition: For $k,n\ge1$, the homotopy group $\pi_k(S^n)$ is the set of [homotopy](c:homotopy) classes of continuous maps $S^k\to S^n$ that keep the base point fixed, where $S^n$ is the [sphere](c:sphere). The product $[f][g]$ performs $f$ on one half of the cube $I^k$ and $g$ on the other half, and the group is abelian for $k\ge2$. It is the [homotopy group](c:homotopy-group) $\pi_k(X)$ of the space $X=S^n$.
examples: We have $\pi_k(S^n)=0$ for $k<n$, and $\pi_n(S^n)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, generated by the identity map.
The Hopf map gives $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, so the groups for $k>n$ need not vanish.
Non-example: the homology group $H_3(S^2)$ is $0$ and is not $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, so homology does not compute $\pi_k(S^n)$.

steps: Let $X$ be a pointed space, and let $\pi_k(X)$ be the set of homotopy classes of pointed maps $S^k\to X$.
Choose $X$ to be the sphere $S^n$.
Then $\pi_k(X)$ is $\pi_k(S^n)$, with the same group law.
links.why: It shows that the homotopy groups of spheres are the general homotopy groups for the test space $S^n$.

reminder: A functor is homotopy invariant when homotopic maps give the same morphism.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $F$ from [topological spaces](c:topological-space) to some category is homotopy invariant when $F(f)=F(g)$ for all [homotopic](c:homotopy) maps $f\simeq g:X\to Y$. Equivalently, $F$ sends the projection $X\times I\to X$ to an isomorphism for every space $X$, where $I$ is the [unit interval](c:interval).
examples: Singular cohomology $H^n(-;A)$ is homotopy invariant: homotopic maps induce the same map in cohomology.
The functor $X\mapsto\pi_0(X)$ that gives the path components is homotopy invariant.

Non-example: the forgetful functor from spaces to sets is not homotopy invariant, because the constant maps $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with values $0$ and $1$ are homotopic but are different functions.

steps: Take a homotopy invariant functor $F$ on spaces.
It is a [functor](c:functor), so it preserves composition and identities.
It satisfies the extra condition that homotopic maps go to the same morphism.
links.why: It shows that homotopy invariance is one extra condition on a functor out of spaces.

reminder: The homotopy limit of a diagram is its limit taken in a way that respects weak equivalences of diagrams.
definition: Let $C$ be a [model category](c:model-category) and $J$ a small category. The homotopy limit $\mathrm{holim}\,D$ of a diagram $D:J\to C$ is the ordinary [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of a fibrant replacement of $D$ in the category of diagrams, and it is the right [derived functor](c:derived-functor) of the limit. It is defined up to weak equivalence, and an objectwise weak equivalence of diagrams induces a weak equivalence of homotopy limits.
examples: The homotopy limit of a cospan $X\to Z\leftarrow Y$ is the homotopy pullback: replace one map by a fibration and take the ordinary pullback.
Over a discrete index category, the homotopy limit of spaces is the product of the spaces.
The homotopy fixed points $X^{hG}$ of a group action are the homotopy limit of the diagram over $BG$ that the action defines.
Non-example: for the diagram $*\to X\leftarrow *$ with $X$ path connected, the ordinary limit is a point, but the homotopy limit is the loop space $\Omega X$.

steps: Take a category $C$ and call only its isomorphisms weak equivalences.
Then a weakly equivalent replacement of a diagram is just an isomorphic diagram.
So the homotopy limit of $D$ is the ordinary [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of $D$.
The general case allows more weak equivalences, and so a finer notion of limit.
links.why: It shows that the homotopy limit reduces to the ordinary limit when weak equivalences are isomorphisms.

steps: Take the category $J$ with three objects and two arrows $a\to c\leftarrow b$.
A diagram of shape $J$ is a cospan $X\to Z\leftarrow Y$.
Replace one of its maps by a fibration and take the ordinary pullback.
The result is the homotopy limit of the cospan, which is the [homotopy pullback](c:homotopy-pullback).
links.why: It shows that a homotopy pullback is the homotopy limit over a cospan.

steps: The limit is a functor $\lim:C^J\to C$ from diagrams to objects.
Replace each diagram by a fibrant one before applying $\lim$.
This gives the right [derived functor](c:derived-functor) of $\lim$, which is the homotopy limit.
links.why: It shows that homotopy limits follow the general rules of derived functors.

reminder: A homotopy operator $h$ satisfies $dh+hd=\mathrm{id}-\pi$, so $\mathrm{id}$ and $\pi$ induce the same map on cohomology.
definition: Let $(C^\bullet,d)$ be a [chain complex](c:chain-complex), for example the [de Rham complex](c:de-rham-complex) of [differential forms](c:differential-form) on a [star-shaped domain](c:star-domain) $U$. A homotopy operator is a family of linear maps $h:C^k\to C^{k-1}$ with $dh+hd=\mathrm{id}-\pi$ in every degree, where $\pi$ is a chain map that is $0$ in positive degrees. On forms over $U$, the map $\pi$ sends a function to its value at the centre, so every closed form of positive degree is exact.
examples: On a star-shaped domain with centre $0$, the operator $(h\omega)_x=\int_0^1t^{k-1}\,\iota_x\omega_{tx}\,dt$, built from the [interior product](c:interior-product) $\iota_x$, is a homotopy operator on $k$-forms.
For homotopic maps $f\simeq g:X\to Y$, the prism operator $P:C_n(X)\to C_{n+1}(Y)$ on singular chains satisfies $\partial P+P\partial=g_\#-f_\#$.
Non-example: the exterior derivative $d$ raises the degree by one, so it is not a homotopy operator, which lowers the degree by one.

steps: Let $h$ be a homotopy operator with $dh+hd=\mathrm{id}-\pi$ on a complex $C$.
Then $h$ is a [chain homotopy](c:chain-homotopy) between the identity map and the chain map $\pi$.
So the identity and $\pi$ induce the same map on cohomology.
In positive degrees $\pi=0$, so the cohomology of $C$ vanishes there.
links.why: It shows how a homotopy operator proves that cohomology vanishes, as in the Poincaré lemma.

reminder: A homotopy pushout is a pushout computed after replacing one of the two maps by a cofibration.
definition: Let $A\leftarrow C\to B$ be a span of spaces with maps $f:C\to A$ and $g:C\to B$. Its homotopy pushout is the double mapping cylinder, the quotient of $A\sqcup(C\times[0,1])\sqcup B$ that glues $(c,0)$ to $f(c)$ and $(c,1)$ to $g(c)$. It is the ordinary [pushout](c:pushout) after the maps are replaced by [cofibrations](c:cofibration), and in a [model category](c:model-category) it is unique up to weak equivalence.
examples: The homotopy pushout of $*\leftarrow A\to *$ is the unreduced suspension of $A$, so for $A=S^{n-1}$ it is $S^n$.
The homotopy pushout of $*\leftarrow A\to X$ is the mapping cone of the map $A\to X$.
If one map is a cofibration, for example $S^{n-1}\to D^n$, the ordinary pushout already is the homotopy pushout.
Non-example: the ordinary pushout of $*\leftarrow S^{n-1}\to *$ is a point and not $S^n$, because neither map is a cofibration.

steps: Take a category $C$ and call only its isomorphisms weak equivalences.
Then every map is a cofibration and replacing a span changes nothing.
So the homotopy pushout of a span is its ordinary [pushout](c:pushout).
links.why: It shows that the homotopy pushout reduces to the ordinary pushout when weak equivalences are isomorphisms.

steps: A span $A\leftarrow C\to B$ is a diagram over the category with three objects and two arrows out of the middle one.
The [homotopy colimit](c:homotopy-colimit) of this diagram replaces it by a cofibrant diagram and takes the colimit.
For this shape the colimit is a pushout, so the homotopy colimit is the homotopy pushout.
links.why: It shows that homotopy pushouts are the homotopy colimits over spans.

reminder: A Hopf algebroid is a bialgebroid together with an antipode that plays the role of inversion in a groupoid.
definition: A Hopf algebroid is a [bialgebroid](c:bialgebroid) with an antipode. In the commutative case, it is a pair $(A,\Gamma)$ of [commutative rings](c:commutative-ring) with source and target maps $\eta_L,\eta_R:A\to\Gamma$, a coproduct $\Gamma\to\Gamma\otimes_A\Gamma$, a counit $\Gamma\to A$ and an antipode $\Gamma\to\Gamma$ that swaps $\eta_L$ and $\eta_R$. These maps satisfy the axioms of a [groupoid](c:groupoid) with the arrows reversed, so $A$ is the ring of objects and $\Gamma$ is the ring of morphisms.
examples: Every commutative [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) $H$ over a ring $k$ gives the Hopf algebroid $(k,H)$, where $\eta_L$ and $\eta_R$ are both the unit map.
For a commutative $k$-algebra $A$, the pair $(A,A\otimes_kA)$ is a Hopf algebroid, with antipode $a\otimes b\mapsto b\otimes a$; it is the pair groupoid.
In stable homotopy theory, the pairs $(MU_*,MU_*MU)$ and $(BP_*,BP_*BP)$ are Hopf algebroids.

Non-example: the monoid algebra $k[t]$ of $(\mathbb{N},+)$, with $\Delta t=t\otimes t$ and $\varepsilon(t)=1$, is a bialgebra but not a Hopf algebra, because an antipode would need an inverse of $t$ in $k[t]$.

steps: Take a Hopf algebroid, which has a coproduct and a counit.
Forget the antipode, and keep the rest of the structure.
What remains is a [bialgebroid](c:bialgebroid).
The Hopf case adds the antipode, which inverts the arrows of the groupoid.
links.why: It shows that a Hopf algebroid is a bialgebroid with inverses.

steps: Let $H$ be a [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) over a commutative ring $k$, and take the base ring to be $k$.
Let the source and target maps both be the unit of $H$.
The coproduct, counit and antipode of $H$ then satisfy the axioms of a Hopf algebroid.
So $H$ is a Hopf algebroid over $k$.
links.why: It shows that a Hopf algebra is a Hopf algebroid with a trivial base.

steps: Let $(A,\Gamma)$ be a [commutative Hopf algebroid](c:commutative-hopf-algebroid).
The rings $A$ and $\Gamma$ are commutative, so $\Gamma$ is an $A$-bimodule through $\eta_L$ and $\eta_R$.
The structure maps satisfy the axioms of a bialgebroid with an antipode.
So $(A,\Gamma)$ is a Hopf algebroid, and the general notion drops the commutativity of the rings.
links.why: It shows that the commutative case is the one used for groupoid schemes.

reminder: A square matrix is Hurwitz when every eigenvalue has a negative real part.
definition: A [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A$ with real or complex entries is a Hurwitz matrix, also called a stable matrix, when every [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) $\lambda$ of $A$ has negative [real part](c:real-part), that is $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda<0$. Equivalently, every solution of $\dot x=Ax$ tends to $0$ as $t\to\infty$. This is the stability sense of the word, and not the coefficient matrix of the Routh-Hurwitz test.
examples: The matrix $-I$ and every diagonal matrix with negative entries are Hurwitz.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-1&5\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$ is Hurwitz, because its eigenvalues are $-1$ and $-2$.
Non-example: the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has the eigenvalues $\pm i$ with real part $0$, so it is not Hurwitz.

reminder: A first-order system of PDE is hyperbolic when its coefficient matrix has real eigenvalues and a full set of real eigenvectors.
definition: A first-order system $u_t+\sum_jA_j(x,t,u)\,\partial_{x_j}u=0$ of [partial differential equations](c:partial-differential-equation) is hyperbolic when, for every real vector $\xi$, the matrix $\sum_j\xi_jA_j$ has only real [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) and a basis of [eigenvectors](c:eigenvector). A second-order linear equation is hyperbolic when the matrix of its second-order coefficients has no zero eigenvalue, one eigenvalue of one sign, and all other eigenvalues of the opposite sign.
examples: The wave equation $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ is hyperbolic, because its coefficient matrix has one positive and one negative eigenvalue.
The advection equation $u_t+au_x=0$ is hyperbolic, because the $1\times1$ matrix $a$ has the real eigenvalue $a$.
Non-example: the Laplace equation $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ is elliptic, because both eigenvalues of its coefficient matrix are positive.

steps: Take a hyperbolic equation or system.
It relates an unknown function to its partial derivatives, so it is a [partial differential equation](c:partial-differential-equation).
The hyperbolic case adds a condition on the eigenvalues of the principal part.
links.why: It shows that hyperbolicity is a condition on the highest-order terms of a PDE.

steps: Write the [wave equation](c:wave-equation) as $u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}=0$ in the variables $(t,x)$.
Its coefficient matrix is $\mathrm{diag}(1,-c^2)$, with one positive and one negative eigenvalue.
So the wave equation is hyperbolic.
A general hyperbolic PDE keeps this sign pattern but allows variable coefficients, lower-order terms and systems.
links.why: It shows that hyperbolic PDE extend the wave equation and keep its finite propagation speeds.

reminder: A hypergraph has a set of vertices and a set of hyperedges, and each hyperedge is a set of vertices.
definition: A hypergraph $H=(V,E)$ consists of a [set](c:set) $V$ of vertices and a [family](c:family) $E$ of subsets of $V$ called hyperedges. A hyperedge may contain any number of vertices. In a $k$-uniform hypergraph, every hyperedge has exactly $k$ vertices.
examples: The Fano plane has $7$ vertices and $7$ hyperedges, and each hyperedge has $3$ vertices.
Every [graph](c:graph) is a hypergraph in which every hyperedge has two vertices.
Non-example: on the vertex set $V=\{1,2,3\}$, a family with the hyperedge $\{1,6\}$ is not a hypergraph, because every hyperedge must be a subset of $V$.

steps: Take a [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$.
Each edge joins two vertices, so it is a $2$-element subset of $V$.
So $(V,E)$ is a hypergraph in which every hyperedge has size $2$.
A general hypergraph allows hyperedges of any size.
links.why: It shows that graphs are the $2$-uniform hypergraphs.

reminder: The $I$-adic filtration of a module $M$ is the chain $M\supseteq IM\supseteq I^2M\supseteq\cdots$ of submodules.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring), $I$ an [ideal](c:ideal) of $R$ and $M$ an $R$-[module](c:module). The $I$-adic filtration of $M$ is the decreasing chain of [submodules](c:submodule) $M\supseteq IM\supseteq I^2M\supseteq\cdots$, where $I^nM$ is generated by the products $a_1\cdots a_nm$ with $a_i\in I$ and $m\in M$.
examples: For $R=M=\mathbb{Z}$ and $I=(p)$, the filtration is $\mathbb{Z}\supseteq p\mathbb{Z}\supseteq p^2\mathbb{Z}\supseteq\cdots$.
For $R=M=k[x]$ and $I=(x)$, the term $I^nM$ is the set of polynomials that $x^n$ divides.

Non-example: the chain $\mathbb{Z}\supseteq6\mathbb{Z}\supseteq12\mathbb{Z}\supseteq18\mathbb{Z}\supseteq\cdots$ is not $I$-adic, because the first step forces $I=(6)$, and then $I^2M=36\mathbb{Z}\ne12\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: The submodules $I^nM$ form a chain, because $I^{n+1}M\subseteq I^nM$.
So $(I^nM)_{n\ge0}$ is a decreasing [filtration](c:filtration) of $M$ by subobjects.
It is special because each step is the previous step multiplied by the one ideal $I$.
links.why: It shows that the $I$-adic filtration is a filtration whose steps are the powers of one ideal.

reminder: The idele class group of a global field is the group of ideles divided by the multiplicative group of the field.
definition: Let $K$ be a [global field](c:global-field). The [group of ideles](c:group-of-ideles) $\mathbb{I}_K$, a [restricted product](c:restricted-product) of the groups $K_v^\times$ over the [places](c:place) $v$ of $K$, consists of the families $(x_v)$ with $x_v$ a unit for almost all finite $v$. The idele class group is the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $C_K=\mathbb{I}_K/K^\times$, where $K^\times$ sits in $\mathbb{I}_K$ diagonally.
examples: For $K=\mathbb{Q}$, the idele class group is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}_{>0}\times\hat{\mathbb{Z}}^\times$.
By Artin reciprocity, for a finite abelian extension $L/K$ the quotient of $C_K$ by the norm group of $L$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$.
Non-example: the family $(x_p)$ with $x_p=p\in\mathbb{Q}_p^\times$ for every prime $p$ is not an idele of $\mathbb{Q}$, because $x_p$ is not a unit for infinitely many $p$.

reminder: The identity type of two terms $a$ and $b$ of type $A$ is a type whose terms are proofs that they are equal.
definition: In [dependent type theory](c:dependent-type-theory), for a type $A$ and terms $a,b:A$, the identity type $a=_Ab$ is a [dependent type](c:dependent-type) over $b$, and its terms are the proofs, or paths, that $a$ equals $b$. It has one constructor, [refl](c:refl), with $\mathrm{refl}_a:a=_Aa$. Its elimination rule, path induction, proves a property of all $p:a=_Ab$ by proving it for $\mathrm{refl}_a$.
examples: For $a:A$, the term $\mathrm{refl}_a$ proves $a=_Aa$; in $\mathbb{N}$, the term $\mathrm{refl}_4$ proves $2+2=_{\mathbb{N}}4$, because both sides compute to $4$.
In homotopy type theory, a term of $a=_Ab$ is a path from $a$ to $b$ in the space $A$.
Non-example: the judgemental equality $a\equiv b$ is not an identity type; it is a judgement of the theory and not a type, so one cannot assume it or quantify over it.

steps: Fix a type $A$ and a term $a:A$.
The family $b\mapsto(a=_Ab)$ of types indexed by $b:A$ has one constructor, $\mathrm{refl}_a:a=_Aa$.
A type family given by constructors of this kind is an [inductive family](c:inductive-family).
Its elimination rule is path induction.
links.why: It shows that path induction is the induction principle of an inductive family.

reminder: An imaginary quadratic field is the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$ for a positive square-free integer $d$.
definition: An imaginary quadratic field is a [field extension](c:field-extension) $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$ of the [rational numbers](c:rational-number), where $d$ is a positive square-free [integer](c:integer). Its elements are the numbers $a+b\sqrt{-d}$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Q}$. It has degree $2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, and it has no embedding into the [real numbers](c:real-number), because $-d<0$.
examples: The field $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ with $d=1$ and the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3})$ with $d=3$ are imaginary quadratic fields.
Exactly nine imaginary quadratic fields have class number $1$: those with $d=1,2,3,7,11,19,43,67,163$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ is a real quadratic field, because $2>0$ and the field embeds in $\mathbb{R}$.

steps: Take $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$, which is generated over $\mathbb{Q}$ by the algebraic number $\sqrt{-d}$.
The element $\sqrt{-d}$ is a root of $x^2+d$, so $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=2$ is finite.
A finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is a [number field](c:number-field).
The imaginary quadratic case adds degree $2$ and $d>0$.
links.why: It shows that every result on number fields applies to imaginary quadratic fields.

reminder: An imaginary unit is a complex number whose square is $-1$.
definition: The imaginary units are the two [complex numbers](c:complex-number) $+i$ and $-i$ that solve the [equation](c:equation) $x^2=-1$. By convention $i$ names one of them, and every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a$ and $b$ [real numbers](c:real-number).
examples: We have $i^2=(-i)^2=-1$, so both $i$ and $-i$ are imaginary units.
In the plane model $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}^2$, multiplication by $i$ turns the plane by $90$ degrees.
Non-example: no real number is an imaginary unit, because every real square is non-negative.
Non-example: $2i$ is not an imaginary unit, because $(2i)^2=-4$.

steps: Take $i$ with $i^2=-1$.
Then $i^4=(i^2)^2=1$, so $i$ is a [root of unity](c:root-of-unity).
Also $i^2=-1\ne1$, so $i$ has order exactly $4$.
So the imaginary units are the primitive fourth roots of unity.
links.why: It shows that the imaginary units are the roots of unity of order four.

reminder: The incircle of a polygon is a circle inside the polygon that touches every side.
definition: The incircle of a [polygon](c:polygon) is a [circle](c:circle) inside the polygon that is [tangent](c:tangent) to every side. Every [triangle](c:triangle) has exactly one incircle; it is the largest circle inside the triangle, and its centre is where the [angle bisectors](c:angle-bisector) meet. A polygon with more sides has an incircle only when such a circle exists.
examples: The incircle of the equilateral triangle with side $a$ has radius $a\sqrt3/6$.
The $3$-$4$-$5$ right triangle with legs on the axes has the incircle with centre $(1,1)$ and radius $1$.
Non-example: a rectangle that is not a square has no incircle, because a circle that touches both pairs of opposite sides would need a diameter equal to both side lengths.

steps: Let $\omega$ be the incircle of a polygon $P$.
Then $\omega$ is a [circle](c:circle) in the plane of $P$, with a centre and a radius.
The incircle adds two conditions: $\omega$ lies inside $P$ and touches every side.
links.why: It shows that an incircle is a circle with two extra conditions, so circle facts apply to it.

reminder: An ind-coherent sheaf is an object of the category that freely adds filtered colimits to the coherent sheaves of a scheme.
definition: Let $X$ be a [scheme](c:scheme) of finite type over a field, and let $\mathrm{Coh}(X)$ be the [dg-category](c:dg-category) of bounded complexes of [coherent sheaves](c:coherent-sheaf). The category $\mathrm{IndCoh}(X)$ is its ind-completion, obtained by freely adding [filtered colimits](c:filtered-colimit). An ind-coherent sheaf is an object of $\mathrm{IndCoh}(X)$, that is, a formal filtered colimit of objects of $\mathrm{Coh}(X)$, an [ind-object](c:ind-object).
examples: Every coherent sheaf, seen as a complex in degree $0$, is an ind-coherent sheaf.
For a smooth scheme $X$ over a field of characteristic $0$, the category $\mathrm{IndCoh}(X)$ agrees with the derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves.

Non-example: a sheaf of $\mathcal{O}$-modules that is not quasi-coherent, such as the extension by zero of $\mathcal{O}$ from $\mathbb{A}^1\setminus\{0\}$ to $\mathbb{A}^1$, gives no object of $\mathrm{IndCoh}(\mathbb{A}^1)$.

steps: Let $\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Coh}(X)$ be the dg-category of bounded coherent complexes.
An [ind-object](c:ind-object) of $\mathcal{C}$ is a formal filtered colimit of objects of $\mathcal{C}$.
By definition, $\mathrm{IndCoh}(X)$ is the category of ind-objects of $\mathcal{C}$.
So every ind-coherent sheaf is an ind-object of $\mathrm{Coh}(X)$.
links.why: It shows that ind-coherent sheaves follow the general rules of ind-objects.

steps: Let $F$ be a [coherent sheaf](c:coherent-sheaf) on $X$, seen as a complex in degree $0$.
It is an object of $\mathrm{Coh}(X)$, so it gives an ind-object by the constant filtered system.
The functor $\mathrm{Coh}(X)\to\mathrm{IndCoh}(X)$ is fully faithful, so no information is lost.
Hence $F$ is an ind-coherent sheaf.
links.why: It shows that ind-coherent sheaves contain the coherent sheaves and add their filtered colimits.

reminder: A family of subsets is independent when every finite intersection of members or complements, using each member once, is non-empty.
definition: Let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ be a [family](c:family) of [subsets](c:subset) of a [set](c:set) $X$. The family is independent when, for all disjoint finite sets $J,K\subseteq I$, the intersection of the sets $A_j$ for $j\in J$ with the [complements](c:complement) $X\setminus A_k$ for $k\in K$ is not empty. So the sets satisfy no relation of a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) except the trivial ones.
examples: In $X=\{0,1\}^3$, the three sets $A_i=\{x:x_i=1\}$ are independent, because every pattern of the three coordinates occurs.
On $X=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$, the coordinate sets $A_n=\{x:x_n=1\}$ form an independent family with countably many members.
Non-example: the sets $A=\{1,2\}$ and $B=\{1,2,3\}$ in $X=\{1,2,3,4\}$ are not independent, because $A\cap(X\setminus B)$ is empty.

reminder: A process has independent increments when its changes over disjoint time intervals are independent random variables.
definition: A [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ has independent increments when, for all times $0\le t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments $X_{t_1}-X_{t_0},\dots,X_{t_n}-X_{t_{n-1}}$ are [independent random variables](c:independent-random-variables). The same definition applies to a discrete-time process $(X_n)$.
examples: [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) has independent increments: $B_t-B_s$ is independent of the past and has the normal distribution with variance $t-s$.
A [random walk](c:random-walk) $S_n=\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_n$ with independent steps has independent increments, because disjoint blocks of steps are independent.
Non-example: $X_t=tZ$ for a non-constant random variable $Z$ has dependent increments, because increments over disjoint intervals are multiples of the same $Z$.

steps: Let $B$ be a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion), so $B_t-B_s$ is independent of the history up to time $s$.
Then increments over disjoint intervals are independent.
So $B$ has independent increments.
Brownian motion also has Gaussian increments and continuous paths, which the general notion does not require.
links.why: It shows that independence of increments is the first property of Brownian motion that results use.

steps: Let $N$ be a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) with rate $\lambda$.
By definition, the counts $N_t-N_s$ over disjoint intervals are independent.
So $N$ has independent increments.
A Poisson process also has Poisson distributed increments, which the general notion does not require.
links.why: It shows that Poisson processes and Brownian motion share the independence of increments.

reminder: An independent set of a graph is a set of vertices, no two of which are joined by an edge.
definition: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a [graph](c:graph). A subset $S\subseteq V$ of [vertices](c:vertex) is an independent set when no [edge](c:edge) of $G$ has both of its ends in $S$. The largest size of an independent set is the independence number $\alpha(G)$.
examples: In the $5$-cycle $C_5$ with the vertices $1,\dots,5$ in order, $\{1,3\}$ is an independent set, and $\alpha(C_5)=2$.
In the complete graph $K_n$, the independent sets are the empty set and the single vertices.
Non-example: in the path $a-b-c$, the set $\{a,b\}$ is not independent, because the edge $ab$ has both ends in it.

reminder: The index of an isolated zero of a vector field is the degree of its direction map on a small sphere around the zero.
definition: Let $v$ be a continuous [vector field](c:vector-field) on an $n$-dimensional [manifold](c:manifold), and let $p$ be an isolated zero of $v$, that is, $v(p)=0$ and $v\ne0$ at all other points near $p$. In a chart around $p$, the index of $v$ at $p$ is the [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of the map $x\mapsto v(x)/|v(x)|$ from a small [sphere](c:sphere) around $p$ to the unit sphere $S^{n-1}$. The index does not depend on the chart or on the radius of the small sphere.
examples: For $v(x)=x$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the zero $0$ has index $1$, because the direction map is the identity of $S^{n-1}$.
For $v(x,y)=(x,-y)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, the saddle at $0$ has index $-1$.
For $v(x)=-x$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the zero $0$ has index $(-1)^n$.
Non-example: the field $v(x,y)=(x,0)$ vanishes on the whole $y$-axis, so its zeros are not isolated and have no index.

steps: Take an isolated zero $p$ of a vector field $v$ and a small sphere $S$ around $p$.
The map $v/|v|$ sends $S$ to the unit sphere, and both are spheres of dimension $n-1$.
The [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of this map is the index of $p$.
So the index is the degree of one particular map between spheres.
links.why: It shows that the index counts how often the direction of the field covers the sphere, with signs.

reminder: The inertia degree of a prime $\mathfrak{P}$ over $\mathfrak{p}$ is the degree of the residue field extension of $\mathfrak{P}$ over $\mathfrak{p}$.
definition: Let $L/K$ be an extension of [number fields](c:number-field), let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) of the [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $\mathcal{O}_K$, and let $\mathfrak{P}$ be a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_L$ that contains $\mathfrak{p}$. The inertia degree $f(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})$ is the [degree](c:degree-of-an-extension) $[\mathcal{O}_L/\mathfrak{P}:\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}]$ of the extension of the [residue fields](c:residue-field). In the fundamental identity $\sum_{\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}}e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})f(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=[L:K]$, the number $e$ is the ramification index.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ the prime $3$ stays prime, and $\mathbb{Z}[i]/(3)\cong\mathbb{F}_9$, so $f=2$.
The prime $5=(2+i)(2-i)$ splits in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, and each factor has residue field $\mathbb{F}_5$, so $f=1$.
Non-example: the number $2$ for the prime $2=-i(1+i)^2$ in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is the ramification index and not the inertia degree, because $\mathbb{Z}[i]/(1+i)\cong\mathbb{F}_2$ gives $f=1$.

steps: Let $k(\mathfrak{p})=\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}$ and $k(\mathfrak{P})=\mathcal{O}_L/\mathfrak{P}$ be the residue fields.
The inclusion $\mathcal{O}_K\to\mathcal{O}_L$ makes $k(\mathfrak{P})$ a field extension of $k(\mathfrak{p})$.
The [degree](c:degree-of-an-extension) of this extension is the inertia degree.
So the inertia degree is the degree of a field extension, applied to residue fields.
links.why: It shows that the inertia degree is a field degree, so the tower law applies to it.

reminder: An infinite loop space is a pointed space with a delooping, whose delooping has a delooping, and so on without end.
definition: A pointed [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is an infinite loop space when there are pointed spaces $X_0=X,X_1,X_2,\dots$ with weak equivalences $X_n\to\Omega X_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge0$, where $\Omega$ forms the [loop space](c:loop-space). Equivalently, $X$ has a [delooping](c:delooping) $X_1$, which has a delooping $X_2$, and so on. Such a sequence is an [Omega-spectrum](c:omega-spectrum), and $X$ is its zeroth space.
examples: Every [Eilenberg-MacLane space](c:eilenberg-maclane-space) $K(A,n)$ with $A$ abelian is an infinite loop space, because $\Omega K(A,n+1)\simeq K(A,n)$.
The space $BU\times\mathbb{Z}$ is an infinite loop space by Bott periodicity, as the zeroth space of complex K-theory.
The space $QX=\mathrm{colim}_n\,\Omega^n\Sigma^nX$ is an infinite loop space for every pointed space $X$.
Non-example: the sphere $S^2$ is not even a loop space, because every loop space is an [H-space](c:h-space), and $S^n$ is an H-space only for $n=0,1,3,7$.

steps: Let $X$ be an infinite loop space, so $X\simeq\Omega X_1$ for some pointed space $X_1$.
Then $X$ is a [loop space](c:loop-space).
The infinite case adds that $X_1$, and every later delooping, is again a loop space.
links.why: It shows that an infinite loop space is a loop space whose delooping can be repeated forever.

reminder: A smooth map is infinitesimally stable when every vector field along it splits into one from the source and one from the target.
definition: Let $f:N\to P$ be a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold). It is infinitesimally stable when every smooth vector field $w$ along $f$, that is, every smooth section of the pullback of the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle) of $P$, has the form $w=df\circ\xi+\eta\circ f$. Here $\xi$ is a [vector field](c:vector-field) on $N$ and $\eta$ is a vector field on $P$.
examples: Every submersion is infinitesimally stable, because $df$ is onto and one can solve $w=df\circ\xi$ with $\eta=0$.
The fold map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y^2)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is infinitesimally stable.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto x^3$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is not infinitesimally stable, because every $3x^2\xi(x)+\eta(x^3)$ has derivative $0$ at $x=0$, but the field $w(x)=x$ has derivative $1$.

reminder: A map $f$ on a partially ordered set is inflationary when $x\le f(x)$ for every element $x$.
definition: Let $(P,\le)$ be a [partially ordered](c:partial-order) set. A [function](c:function) $f:P\to P$ is inflationary, also called extensive or progressive, when $x\le f(x)$ for every $x\in P$. It need not be monotone, and it need not be idempotent.
examples: On $\mathbb{N}$, the successor map $n\mapsto n+1$ is inflationary, and so is every map with $f(n)\ge n$.
The topological closure $A\mapsto\overline{A}$ on the subsets of a space, ordered by inclusion, is inflationary.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto x/2$ on the positive real numbers is not inflationary, because $x\le x/2$ is false.

steps: Let $c$ be a [closure operator](c:closure-operator) on a partially ordered set $P$.
By definition, $x\le c(x)$ for every $x$, so $c$ is inflationary.
A closure operator is also monotone and idempotent, which a general inflationary map need not be.
links.why: It shows that closure operators are the inflationary maps that are also monotone and idempotent.

reminder: An initial algebra of an endofunctor is an algebra with exactly one algebra map to every other algebra.
definition: Let $F:C\to C$ be an [endofunctor](c:endofunctor). An initial algebra of $F$ is an [initial object](c:initial-object) of the category of [algebras](c:algebra-for-an-endofunctor) for $F$: an algebra $(A,\alpha:F(A)\to A)$ such that, for every algebra $(B,\beta)$, exactly one morphism $h:A\to B$ has $h\circ\alpha=\beta\circ F(h)$. The structure map $\alpha$ of an initial algebra is an isomorphism (Lambek's lemma), so $A$ is a fixed point of $F$.
examples: For $F(X)=1+X$ on sets, the initial algebra is $\mathbb{N}$ with zero and successor, and the unique map out of it is definition by recursion.
For $F(X)=1+A\times X$ on sets, the initial algebra is the set of finite lists over $A$, with the empty list and the cons operation.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ with zero and successor is an algebra for $F(X)=1+X$ but is not initial, because no algebra map $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{N}$ exists: the element $-1$ would need $f(-1)+1=0$.

steps: Take the category of algebras for $F$ and the algebra morphisms between them.
An initial algebra is an initial object of this category.
So it has exactly one morphism to every algebra, and it is unique up to unique isomorphism.
links.why: It shows that initial algebras are initial objects, so they are unique up to isomorphism.

steps: Let $C$ have a terminal object $1$ and binary coproducts, and let $F(X)=1+X$.
An algebra for $F$ is an object $B$ with a point $b:1\to B$ and an endomorphism $g:B\to B$.
An initial algebra $(N,0,s)$ has a unique map to every such $(B,b,g)$, which is definition by recursion.
That is a [natural numbers object](c:natural-numbers-object).
links.why: It shows that the natural numbers are the initial algebra of the functor that adds a point.

reminder: The injectivity radius at $p$ is the largest $r$ such that the exponential map at $p$ is a diffeomorphism on the $r$-ball.
definition: Let $(M,g)$ be a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) and $p\in M$, and let $\exp_p$ be the [exponential map](c:exponential-map) at $p$. The injectivity radius $\mathrm{inj}(p)$ is the supremum of all $r>0$ such that $\exp_p$ restricted to the open ball $B_r(0)$ of the [tangent space](c:tangent-space) $T_pM$ is a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) onto its image. The injectivity radius of $M$ is the infimum of $\mathrm{inj}(p)$ over all $p\in M$.
examples: The unit round sphere $S^n$ has injectivity radius $\pi$.
The flat torus $\mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$ has injectivity radius $1/2$, which is half the length of its shortest closed geodesic.
Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has injectivity radius $\infty$.
Non-example: the distance to the first conjugate point is not the injectivity radius, because the flat torus has no conjugate points and its injectivity radius is $1/2$.

reminder: An inner automorphism of a group $G$ is conjugation $h\mapsto ghg^{-1}$ by a fixed element $g$ of $G$.
definition: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group) and $g\in G$. The inner automorphism $\phi_g:G\to G$ is the map $\phi_g(h)=ghg^{-1}$, that is, [conjugation](c:conjugation) by $g$. The inner automorphisms form a normal subgroup $\mathrm{Inn}(G)$ of the [automorphism group](c:automorphism-group) $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$, and $\mathrm{Inn}(G)\cong G/Z(G)$, where $Z(G)$ is the centre.
examples: In the symmetric group $S_3$, conjugation by $(12)$ fixes $(12)$ and swaps $(13)$ and $(23)$.
In an abelian group, every inner automorphism is the identity.
In $GL_n(k)$, conjugation by an invertible matrix $P$ is the change of basis $A\mapsto PAP^{-1}$.
Non-example: the inversion $x\mapsto-x$ is an automorphism of $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ but not an inner one, because every inner automorphism of an abelian group is the identity.

steps: Let $\phi_g(h)=ghg^{-1}$ for a group $G$ and $g\in G$.
It preserves products, because $\phi_g(hk)=ghkg^{-1}=\phi_g(h)\phi_g(k)$.
It is a bijection, with inverse $\phi_{g^{-1}}$.
So $\phi_g$ is an [automorphism](c:automorphism) of $G$.
links.why: It shows why conjugation maps are automorphisms, and so $\mathrm{Inn}(G)$ lies inside $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$.

reminder: A measure is inner regular when the measure of each measurable set is the supremum of the measures of its compact subsets.
definition: A [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on a [topological space](c:topological-space) is inner regular when $\mu(s)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subseteq s,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ for every [measurable set](c:measurable-set) $s$. The supremum runs over the [compact](c:compact-space) subsets $K$ of $s$.
examples: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is inner regular: compact sets approximate each measurable set from inside.
Every finite Borel measure on a complete separable metric space is inner regular.

Non-example: let $X$ be an uncountable discrete space with the countable-cocountable $\sigma$-algebra, and let $\mu$ be $0$ on countable sets and $1$ on cocountable sets; every compact set is finite and null, but $\mu(X)=1$.

steps: Let $\mu$ be a [regular measure](c:regular-measure), so it is both inner regular and outer regular.
The inner half says $\mu(s)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subseteq s\text{ compact}\}$.
So $\mu$ is inner regular.
Inner regularity alone drops the approximation from outside by open sets.
links.why: It shows that regularity is inner regularity plus outer regularity.

steps: Inner regularity asks that $\mu(A)$ be the supremum of $\mu(K)$ over compact $K\subseteq A$, for each set $A$ of a chosen class.
Choose the class of all measurable sets.
Then the property says exactly that $\mu$ is an inner regular measure.
links.why: It shows that an inner regular measure is inner regularity for the class of all measurable sets.

reminder: Inner regularity on a class of sets means that each set's measure is the supremum of the measures of its compact subsets.
definition: Let $\mu$ be a [measure](c:measure) on a [topological space](c:topological-space), and let $\mathcal{A}$ be a class of measurable sets, such as the open sets, the [Borel sets](c:borel-set) or all measurable sets. The measure $\mu$ is inner regular on $\mathcal{A}$ when $\mu(A)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subseteq A,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ for every $A\in\mathcal{A}$, where $K$ is a [compact](c:compact-space) set. Variants ask this only for open sets, or only for sets of finite measure.
examples: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is inner regular on the Borel sets.
A [Radon measure](c:radon-measure) on a locally compact Hausdorff space is inner regular on the open sets.

Non-example: the countable-cocountable $0$-$1$ measure on an uncountable discrete space is not inner regular on the whole space, because every compact subset is finite and null, but the space has measure $1$.

steps: Take the class of all measurable sets.
Inner regularity on this class says $\mu(s)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subseteq s\text{ compact}\}$ for every measurable $s$.
That is the definition of an [inner regular measure](c:inner-regular).
links.why: It shows that the usual notion of an inner regular measure is the case of all measurable sets.

steps: Take the class of measurable sets $s$ with $\mu(s)<\infty$.
Inner regularity on this class says that each such $s$ has $\mu(s)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subseteq s\text{ compact}\}$.
That is a measure that is [inner regular for finite-measure sets](c:inner-regular-compact-lt-top).
links.why: It shows that the finite-measure variant is the case of the class of sets with finite measure.

reminder: The inradius of a triangle is the radius of its incircle.
definition: The inradius $r$ of a [triangle](c:triangle) is the [radius](c:radius) of its [incircle](c:incircle). If the triangle has [area](c:area) $S$ and semiperimeter $s$, half the [perimeter](c:perimeter), then $r=S/s$. A polygon that has an incircle also has an inradius, the radius of that circle.
examples: The $3$-$4$-$5$ right triangle has area $6$ and semiperimeter $6$, so its inradius is $1$.
The equilateral triangle with side $a$ has inradius $a\sqrt3/6$.
The square with side $a$ has inradius $a/2$.
Non-example: the circumradius $R$ is not the inradius; the $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle has $R=5/2$ and $r=1$.

reminder: An instanton is a finite-action field configuration with a non-trivial topological charge, such as a self-dual Yang-Mills connection.
definition: An instanton is a field configuration of a gauge theory that lies outside the connected component of the trivial configuration, because it carries a non-zero topological charge. For a Yang-Mills gauge field, that is, a [connection](c:connection) on a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) over a $4$-manifold, an instanton is a connection of finite action whose [curvature](c:curvature) $F$ is self-dual or anti-self-dual, $F=\pm\star F$. Such a connection minimizes the Yang-Mills action in its topological class.
examples: The [BPST instanton](c:bpst-instanton) is an $SU(2)$ Yang-Mills instanton on $\mathbb{R}^4$ with instanton number $1$ and finite action.
The ADHM construction describes all instantons of a given charge on $S^4$ by linear algebra data.
Non-example: a flat connection on the trivial bundle has charge $0$ and lies in the trivial component, so it is not an instanton.

steps: Let $A$ be a [Yang-Mills instanton](c:yang-mills-instanton), a finite-action connection with $F=\pm\star F$.
Then $\mathrm{tr}(F\wedge F)=\pm|F|^2\,\mathrm{vol}$ up to a constant, so the topological charge is non-zero unless $A$ is flat.
A non-flat self-dual connection therefore lies outside the trivial component.
So $A$ is an instanton in the general sense.
links.why: It shows that the self-dual Yang-Mills connections are the standard instantons of gauge theory.

steps: The [BPST instanton](c:bpst-instanton) is the self-dual $SU(2)$ connection on $\mathbb{R}^4$ with instanton number $1$.
It has finite action and a non-zero topological charge.
So it is an instanton.
links.why: It shows the standard concrete example of an instanton.

reminder: A measurable function is integrable when the integral of its absolute value is finite.
definition: A [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f$ on a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X,\mu)$ is integrable when $\int_X|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, where the integral is the [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral). The number $\int_Xf\,d\mu$ is then defined, and the integrable functions form the space $L^1(\mu)$.
examples: Every continuous function on $[0,1]$ is integrable for Lebesgue measure, because it is bounded.
The function $x^{-1/2}$ on $(0,1)$ is integrable with integral $2$, although it is unbounded.
Non-example: $1/x$ on $(0,1)$ is not integrable, because $\int_0^1dx/x=\infty$.
Non-example: $\sin(x)/x$ on $(0,\infty)$ is not Lebesgue integrable, because $\int|\sin x|/x\,dx=\infty$, although its improper Riemann integral exists.

steps: Let $f$ be Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$.
Then $f$ is bounded and continuous almost everywhere, so $f$ is measurable.
A bounded measurable function on a set of finite measure has $\int|f|<\infty$.
So $f$ is Lebesgue integrable, and the two integrals agree.
links.why: It shows that Lebesgue integrability contains Riemann integrability on bounded intervals.

steps: Take an integrable function $f$.
By definition, $f$ is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function).
It satisfies the extra condition $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$.
links.why: It shows that integrability is one finiteness condition on a measurable function.

reminder: The integral closure of $A$ in $B$ is the set of elements of $B$ that are roots of monic polynomials over $A$.
definition: Let $A\subseteq B$ be [commutative rings](c:commutative-ring). An element $x\in B$ is integral over $A$ when $x$ is a root of a [monic polynomial](c:monic-polynomial) $x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0$ with all $a_i\in A$. The integral closure of $A$ in $B$ is the set of all elements of $B$ that are integral over $A$; it is a [subring](c:subring) of $B$ that contains $A$.
examples: The integral closure of $\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{Z}$, because a rational root of a monic integer polynomial is an integer.
The integral closure of $\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ is $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, and in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt5)$ it is $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt5)/2]$.
Non-example: $1/2$ is not in the integral closure of $\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Q}$, because no monic polynomial with integer coefficients has $1/2$ as a root.

steps: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field), and take $A=\mathbb{Z}$ and $B=K$.
The integral closure of $\mathbb{Z}$ in $K$ is the set of elements of $K$ that are roots of monic integer polynomials.
These elements are the algebraic integers of $K$, and they form the [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $\mathcal{O}_K$.
links.why: It shows that the ring of integers of a number field is an integral closure.

reminder: An integrally closed domain contains every element of its fraction field that is a root of a monic polynomial over the domain.
definition: An [integral domain](c:integral-domain) $A$ is integrally closed when every element of its [field of fractions](c:field-of-fractions) $K$ that is a root of a [monic polynomial](c:monic-polynomial) with coefficients in $A$ already lies in $A$. In other words, the [integral closure](c:integral-closure) of $A$ in $K$ is $A$.
examples: The ring $\mathbb{Z}$ is integrally closed, and so is every [unique factorization domain](c:unique-factorization-domain), such as $k[x,y]$.
The ring of integers of a number field, for example $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, is integrally closed.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt5]$ is not integrally closed, because $(1+\sqrt5)/2$ is a root of $x^2-x-1$ but is not in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt5]$.
Non-example: $k[t^2,t^3]$ is not integrally closed, because $t$ is a root of $X^2-t^2$ but $t\notin k[t^2,t^3]$.

steps: Take an integrally closed domain $A$.
By definition, it is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain), with no zero divisors.
It satisfies the extra condition that its integral closure in its field of fractions is $A$.
links.why: It shows that integral closedness is one extra condition on an integral domain.

steps: Let $A$ be a [unique factorization domain](c:unique-factorization-domain), and let $x=a/b$ with $a,b$ coprime be a root of a monic polynomial over $A$ of degree $n$.
Multiply the equation by $b^n$ to get $a^n=-b\,(c_{n-1}a^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0b^{n-1})$.
So every prime factor of $b$ divides $a^n$, hence divides $a$, which contradicts coprimality unless $b$ is a unit.
Then $x=a/b$ lies in $A$, so $A$ is integrally closed.
links.why: It shows that unique factorization is a sufficient condition for integral closedness.

reminder: Integration assigns to a function the limit of sums of its values times small widths, the signed area under its graph.
definition: Integration is the operation that assigns to an integrable [function](c:function) $f$ on an interval $[a,b]$ the number $\int_a^bf(x)\,dx$, the limit of the sums $\sum_if(t_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})$ as the subdivision of $[a,b]$ gets finer. More generally, one integrates a function over a set $X$ against a [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ to get $\int_Xf\,d\mu$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, integration undoes [differentiation](c:derivative) for continuous functions.
examples: We have $\int_0^1x^2\,dx=1/3$, the area under the parabola on $[0,1]$.
A finite sum $\sum_{x\in X}f(x)$ is the integral of $f$ against the counting measure on $X$.
Non-example: differentiation is not integration; it sends $x^2$ to $2x$, a function and not an accumulated number, and the two operations are inverse to each other.

steps: Let $f$ be Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$.
Its [Riemann integral](c:riemann-integral) is the limit of the sums $\sum_if(t_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})$ as the subdivision gets finer.
This limit is the number that integration assigns to $f$.
General integration extends this idea to measures and to more functions.
links.why: It shows that the Riemann integral is the first and simplest form of integration.

steps: Take Lebesgue measure on $[a,b]$ and a bounded measurable function $f$.
The [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) of $f$ is the supremum of the integrals of simple functions below it.
It agrees with the Riemann integral whenever that exists.
So the Lebesgue integral is integration against a measure.
links.why: It shows that integration against a measure includes the Lebesgue integral and its limit theorems.

reminder: The interior product $\iota_X\omega$ inserts the vector field $X$ into the first slot of the differential form $\omega$.
definition: Let $X$ be a [vector field](c:vector-field) and $\omega$ a [differential form](c:differential-form) of degree $k\ge1$ on a manifold. The interior product $\iota_X\omega$ is the $(k-1)$-form with $(\iota_X\omega)(Y_1,\dots,Y_{k-1})=\omega(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_{k-1})$, and $\iota_Xf=0$ for a function $f$. It is an antiderivation of degree $-1$: $\iota_X(\alpha\wedge\beta)=\iota_X\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{|\alpha|}\alpha\wedge\iota_X\beta$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\iota_{\partial_x}(dx\wedge dy)=dy$ and $\iota_{\partial_y}(dx\wedge dy)=-dx$.
For a $1$-form $\theta$, the form $\iota_X\theta=\theta(X)$ is a function.
Cartan's formula $\mathcal{L}_X=d\iota_X+\iota_Xd$ expresses the [Lie derivative](c:lie-derivative) with the interior product.
Non-example: wedging with a fixed $1$-form $\theta$ is not an interior product, because $\theta\wedge-$ raises the degree by one, and $\iota_X$ lowers it.

steps: A $k$-form is a tensor with $k$ covariant slots that is antisymmetric in them.
A vector field $X$ is a tensor with one contravariant slot.
Contracting $X$ with the first slot of $\omega$ gives $\omega(X,\cdot,\dots,\cdot)$.
That is $\iota_X\omega$, so the interior product is a [tensor contraction](c:tensor-contraction).
links.why: It shows that the interior product is a contraction that keeps antisymmetry.

reminder: A module is the internal direct sum of submodules when each element is uniquely a sum of one element from each.
definition: Let $M_1,\dots,M_n$ be [submodules](c:submodule) of a [module](c:module) $M$, or subgroups of an abelian group, or subspaces of a vector space. Then $M$ is their internal direct sum, written $M=M_1\oplus\cdots\oplus M_n$, when every $m\in M$ can be written in exactly one way as $m=m_1+\cdots+m_n$ with $m_i\in M_i$. Equivalently, $M_1+\cdots+M_n=M$ and each $M_i$ meets the sum of the others only in $0$.
examples: The plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the internal direct sum of the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis.
The group $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ is the internal direct sum of its subgroups $\{0,2,4\}$ and $\{0,3\}$.
Non-example: three distinct lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^2$ add up to $\mathbb{R}^2$, but not uniquely, because each line meets the sum of the other two in a whole line.

steps: Let $M=M_1\oplus\cdots\oplus M_n$ be an internal direct sum.
The map $M_1\times\cdots\times M_n\to M$, $(m_k)\mapsto\sum_km_k$, is a bijection by the unique-sum property.
It is also a homomorphism, so it is an isomorphism from the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of the $M_k$ onto $M$.
So $M$ is a direct sum of the $M_k$, with the extra fact that the summands are subobjects of $M$.
links.why: It shows that an internal direct sum is isomorphic to the external direct sum of its summands.

reminder: The internal hom $[X,Y]$ is an object with $\mathrm{hom}(Z\otimes X,Y)\cong\mathrm{hom}(Z,[X,Y])$ for every object $Z$.
definition: Let $C$ be a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) with tensor product $\otimes$, and let $X$ and $Y$ be [objects](c:object) of $C$. An internal hom $[X,Y]$ is an object of $C$ with a bijection $\mathrm{hom}(Z\otimes X,Y)\cong\mathrm{hom}(Z,[X,Y])$ that is natural in $Z$, so $[X,Y]$ is the object of morphisms from $X$ to $Y$. If it exists for all $X$ and $Y$, then $[X,-]$ is right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) to $-\otimes X$, and $C$ is a [closed monoidal category](c:closed-monoidal-category).
examples: In sets with the cartesian product, $[X,Y]$ is the function set $Y^X$.
In vector spaces with the tensor product, $[X,Y]$ is the space $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)$ of linear maps.

Non-example: in groups with the cartesian product, internal homs do not exist in general, because a cartesian closed category with a zero object is trivial, and groups have a zero object and are not trivial.

steps: Take the cartesian product as the tensor product of $C$.
An internal hom $[X,Y]$ then has $\mathrm{hom}(Z\times X,Y)\cong\mathrm{hom}(Z,[X,Y])$.
That is the defining property of the [exponential object](c:exponential-object) $Y^X$.
links.why: It shows that exponential objects are internal homs for the cartesian product.

steps: Take the category of sets with the cartesian product.
For sets $X$ and $Y$, the functions $Z\times X\to Y$ correspond to the functions $Z\to Y^X$ by currying.
So the [function set](c:function-set) $Y^X$ is an internal hom $[X,Y]$.
links.why: It shows that the function set is the internal hom of the category of sets.

reminder: The intersection pairing sends two middle-degree cohomology classes to the value of their cup product on the fundamental class.
definition: Let $M$ be a closed oriented [manifold](c:manifold) of dimension $2k$ with [fundamental class](c:fundamental-class) $[M]$. The intersection pairing is the form $H^k(M;\mathbb{R})\times H^k(M;\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}$, $(a,b)\mapsto\langle a\cup b,[M]\rangle$, where $a\cup b$ is the [cup product](c:cup-product) in [cohomology](c:cohomology). By Poincaré duality, it counts with signs the points where cycles dual to $a$ and $b$ meet, and it is symmetric for even $k$ and skew-symmetric for odd $k$.
examples: On $\mathbb{CP}^2$, the group $H^2$ is spanned by one class $h$ with $\langle h\cup h,[\mathbb{CP}^2]\rangle=1$, so the pairing is the matrix $(1)$.
On $S^2\times S^2$, the pairing on $H^2$ has the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ in the basis of the two factor classes.
Non-example: a closed $3$-manifold has no such pairing on $H^k$, because the cup product of two classes of degree $k$ has degree $2k\ne3$.

steps: The cup product is bilinear, and evaluation on $[M]$ is linear.
So $(a,b)\mapsto\langle a\cup b,[M]\rangle$ is linear in each argument.
Hence the intersection pairing is a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) on $H^k(M;\mathbb{R})$.
It adds the symmetry $(-1)^k$ and, by Poincaré duality, it is non-degenerate.
links.why: It shows that the intersection pairing is a bilinear form with extra symmetry and non-degeneracy.

reminder: The intrinsic metric of a surface gives the distance between two points as the infimum of lengths of paths inside it.
definition: Let $S$ be a [surface](c:surface) in Euclidean space, or more generally a space in which [curves](c:curve) have a length $L$. The intrinsic metric of $S$ is $d_S(x,y)=\inf L(\gamma)$, where the infimum runs over all curves $\gamma$ in $S$ from $x$ to $y$. It makes a connected $S$ a [metric space](c:metric-space), and unlike the restricted Euclidean [distance](c:distance), it uses only paths that stay in $S$.
examples: On the unit sphere $S^2\subset\mathbb{R}^3$, the intrinsic distance between antipodal points is $\pi$, the length of a half great circle.

On a convex polyhedron, the intrinsic distance between two points is the length of the shortest path over the faces, and Alexandrov's uniqueness theorem says that this metric determines the polyhedron up to congruence.
Non-example: the chord distance restricted from $\mathbb{R}^3$ to the sphere is not its intrinsic metric, because antipodal points have chord distance $2$ but intrinsic distance $\pi$.

reminder: A subset is invariant under a group action when the action maps it into itself.
definition: Let a [group](c:group) or [monoid](c:monoid) $G$ act on a set $X$ by a [group action](c:group-action). A [subset](c:subset) $S\subseteq X$ is an invariant set when $g\cdot s\in S$ for all $g\in G$ and $s\in S$. For a group this means $g\cdot S=S$ for every $g\in G$, because $g^{-1}$ also maps $S$ into $S$.
examples: For the rotations about the origin acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$, every circle centred at the origin is invariant, and so is $\{0\}$.
For the action of $\mathbb{Z}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ by integer translation, the sets $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$ are invariant.
Non-example: a line through the origin is not invariant under the rotations about the origin, because the rotation by $90$ degrees moves it to another line.

steps: Let $x\in X$ and let $G\cdot x=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$ be its [orbit](c:orbit).
For $h\in G$, we have $h\cdot(g\cdot x)=(hg)\cdot x\in G\cdot x$.
So the orbit is an invariant set.
It is the smallest invariant set that contains $x$.
links.why: It shows that invariant sets are the unions of orbits.

steps: Let a linear operator $T$ act on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ through the monoid of its powers $T^n$.
A subspace $W$ is an [invariant subspace](c:invariant-subspace) when $T(W)\subseteq W$.
Then $T^n(W)\subseteq W$ for all $n$, so $W$ is an invariant set of this action.
The invariant subspace adds that $W$ is a linear subspace.
links.why: It shows that an invariant subspace is an invariant set that is also a subspace.

reminder: An inverse system is a family of objects with maps from larger indices to smaller indices that compose consistently.
definition: An inverse system indexed by a [preorder](c:is-preorder) $(I,\le)$ in a [category](c:category) $C$ is a contravariant [functor](c:functor) from $I$ to $C$. Concretely, it consists of objects $X_i$ and morphisms $f_{ij}:X_j\to X_i$ for $i\le j$ with $f_{ii}=\mathrm{id}$ and $f_{ij}\circ f_{jk}=f_{ik}$ for $i\le j\le k$.
examples: The groups $\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$ with the reduction maps $\mathbb{Z}/p^{n+1}\to\mathbb{Z}/p^n$ form an inverse system over $\mathbb{N}$, and its limit is the ring of $p$-adic integers.
For a group $G$, the finite quotients $G/N$ with the quotient maps $G/N'\to G/N$ for $N'\subseteq N$ form an inverse system whose limit is the profinite completion of $G$.
Non-example: take $X_n=\mathbb{Z}$ with $f_{mn}(x)=2x$ for all $m\le n$; this is not an inverse system, because $f_{nn}$ is not the identity.

steps: Take an inverse system $(X_i,f_{ij})$ over a preorder $I$.
View $I$ as a category with one arrow $i\to j$ when $i\le j$.
The assignment $i\mapsto X_i$, $(i\le j)\mapsto f_{ij}$ reverses arrows and respects composition and identities.
So it is a contravariant [functor](c:functor) from $I$ to $C$.
links.why: It shows that an inverse system is a functor on a preorder, so limits of functors apply to it.

reminder: Inversion in a circle with centre $O$ and radius $r$ sends a point $P$ to the point $P'$ on ray $OP$ with $OP\cdot OP'=r^2$.
definition: Let $\omega$ be a [circle](c:circle) with centre $O$ and radius $r$. Inversion in $\omega$ is the map that sends each [point](c:point) $P\ne O$ to the point $P'$ on the ray from $O$ through $P$ with $|OP|\cdot|OP'|=r^2$. It fixes every point of $\omega$, swaps the inside and the outside of $\omega$, and maps circles and [lines](c:line) to circles or lines.
examples: For the unit circle, inversion sends the point $(2,0)$ to $(1/2,0)$ and fixes the point $(0,1)$.
Inversion maps a line that does not pass through $O$ to a circle that passes through $O$.
Non-example: the point reflection $P\mapsto2O-P$ is not an inversion, because it keeps the distance to $O$, while inversion changes $|OP|$ to $r^2/|OP|$.

steps: Let $P'$ be the image of $P$, so $P'$ lies on the ray $OP$ and $|OP|\cdot|OP'|=r^2$.
Invert $P'$: its image $P''$ lies on the same ray, with $|OP''|=r^2/|OP'|=|OP|$.
The two points coincide, so $P''=P$.
Hence inversion applied twice is the identity, so it is an [involution](c:involution).
links.why: It shows that inversion is its own inverse, so it is a bijection of the punctured plane.
